name: Domoda
subtitle: A rich groundnut stew simmered with roasted peanut paste, vegetables and meat, considered the defining comfort food of The Gambia.

facts.label: Staple base
facts.value: Roasted peanut paste (groundnut paste) and tomato puree

parts.text: Domoda is a savory, thick stew made from roasted peanut paste simmered with tomatoes, onions, garlic, and fresh vegetables such as pumpkin, sweet potato, cassava, or bitter tomato (jato).
It is prepared with beef, chicken, or river fish, or made entirely vegetarian.
The signature flavor comes from a delicate balance between the rich, oily sweetness of dark-roasted peanuts and the sharp acidity of fresh lime juice stirred in at the end of cooking.
Domoda is traditionally served over a large communal platter of steamed broken white rice.
Families sit around the dish, spooning the thick sauce over their section of rice and sharing chunks of tender meat and root vegetables.
The dish originates with the Mandinka people of Senegambia.
During the 19th and 20th centuries, groundnuts (peanuts) became the principal agricultural cash crop along the Gambia River, cementing domoda as the national everyday staple across ethnic boundaries.

blocks.title: Gambian Domoda at home
blocks.sub: Adapted from Gambian home cooking methods reported by Saveur and Access Gambia.
blocks.note: Beef chuck can be replaced with chicken or firm pumpkin for a vegetarian version; peanut paste must be unsweetened 100% roasted peanuts.

ingredients.name: beef chuck or stewing beef, cut into 3cm cubes
smooth unsweetened roasted peanut butter (groundnut paste)
butternut squash or pumpkin, peeled and cubed
habanero or Scotch bonnet chilli, left whole for aroma

steps.text: Brown the beef in a heavy-bottomed Dutch oven with oil over medium-high heat until well seared on all sides.
Add chopped onions and minced garlic, sautéing until translucent and fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste, cooking for two minutes until it darkens slightly.
Whisk the peanut butter into warm water until completely smooth, then pour into the pot with the beef.
Drop in the whole chilli, cover partially, and simmer on gentle low heat, stirring frequently to prevent sticking.
Add the cubed pumpkin and simmer until the vegetables and meat are meltingly tender and peanut oil rises to the surface.
Stir in fresh lime juice, season with salt and black pepper, and rest for 10 minutes before serving over hot white rice.

gaps: Regional variations between rural upper-river Mandinka domoda and coastal urban Wolof versions that incorporate smoked bonga fish (kobo) for deeper umami.
Exact historical records documenting when American groundnuts directly replaced indigenous bambara groundnuts in Mandinka cooking during the transatlantic trade era.
